introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde, puis les questions 1 à 12 réparties en quatre sections de trois questions) : filigranes gcerevision.com et texte fantôme du verso (transparence du papier) ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation ni statistique précise n'est avancée ; les dates, noms, traités et lieux sont ceux de l'historiographie établie, cités de mémoire historique et à faire relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Question 3 : le sujet parle de « West Africa » ; le corrigé traite surtout le Nigeria du Nord (Lugard), le Sud-Est nigérian (Women's War de 1929) et l'AOF avec les Quatre Communes du Sénégal. La date de création de l'AOF (1895) et le rôle de Dakar sont donnés sans détail administratif.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Compare and contrast the British policy of Indirect Rule with the French policy of Assimilation in West Africa.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** After the Scramble for Africa the colonial powers had to govern large territories with few officials and little money. Britain generally used Indirect Rule, a system of governing through traditional rulers, associated with Frederick Lugard in Northern Nigeria (from 1900) and set out in his book *The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa* (1922). France in West Africa (the Federation of French West Africa, created in 1895 and governed from Dakar) announced a policy of Assimilation, which aimed at making Africans French in culture and law. The two policies had common aims but different methods.

**1. Similarities.**
- *Same basic aims.* Both served the interests of the colonial power: raw materials, markets and strategic advantage, and both justified rule by a "civilising mission".
- *Use of African intermediaries.* Despite the theory, the French also used chiefs (canton and village chiefs) to collect taxes, recruit labour and keep order, just as the British used emirs, chiefs and "warrant chiefs".
- *Taxation, forced labour and cash crops.* Both imposed a head tax, forced or compulsory labour and the growing of export crops (groundnuts in Senegal, cotton, cocoa and palm produce), and both kept the key decisions in European hands.
- *Racial hierarchy and paternalism.* Africans, with few exceptions, were treated as subjects without the same rights as Europeans, and political parties and the press were controlled.
- *Both changed in practice.* After 1919 the French moved towards "Association", which respected local institutions in practice, while the British introduced reforms after 1945 and in some places (Gold Coast, Southern Nigeria) ran a system that was only partly "indirect".

**2. Differences.**
- *Attitude to African culture.* Indirect Rule kept local institutions, laws and customs, provided they were not "repugnant" to British ideas of justice. Assimilation rejected African culture as inferior and wished to replace it by French language, laws and values.
- *Administrative structure.* The British system was decentralised: Native Authorities, native courts and native treasuries in each emirate or district, under British residents and district officers. The French system was highly centralised: a Governor-General at Dakar, lieutenant-governors, and *cercles* run by commandants who gave orders to appointed chiefs.
- *Role of chiefs.* British rulers kept existing rulers and gave them real local power; where no chiefs existed (as in much of south-eastern Nigeria) chiefs were created ("warrant chiefs"), which caused trouble such as the Women's War of 1929. French chiefs were civil servants with little independent authority and could be dismissed.
- *Citizenship and rights.* The French offered citizenship to those who met strict conditions of education and culture, and the people of the Four Communes of Senegal (Saint-Louis, Gorée, Dakar and Rufisque) had citizens' rights from the nineteenth century (Blaise Diagne became the first African deputy in 1914). Most Africans stayed "subjects" under the *indigénat* code. Britain offered no such route to citizenship, but there were African members of some councils.
- *Education.* French education used the French language and curriculum and produced few "évolués"; British education used mission schools, African languages in the early years and English later.
- *Results.* Indirect Rule was cheap and worked best in the emirates of Northern Nigeria; it kept traditional elites in power and slowed the growth of modern politics there. Assimilation was costly and reached few people, but produced a small group of French-educated leaders (Senghor, Houphouët-Boigny) who later entered French politics.

**Conclusion.** Indirect Rule and Assimilation differed in theory (preservation against transformation, decentralisation against centralisation), but in practice both were systems of control in which Africans had little power. The French became more flexible and the British more interventionist as time went on, so by the 1940s the gap between the two had narrowed, although their legacies for the independence period were different.
